newsitem.title: CANADA: Manitoba evacutes 17,500 people as Red River rises.
newsitem.headline: Manitoba evacutes 17,500 people as Red River rises.

text.p: Manitoba on Wednesday ordered 17,500 people to evacuate their homes as the Red River surged up to four feet in the past 24 hours and a third person was presumed drowned in the rising flood waters.

Daniel Leskiw, 40, of Souris, Manitoba, missing since Tuesday night after he went kayaking on the Souris River, was presumed drowned, according to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. Police said they recovered his life vest and kayak.

Adam Young, 14, of Winnipeg, was also presumed dead after he was swept away by powerful currents in a drainage ditch in Winnipeg on Tuesday, police said. Rescue workers resumed the search for Young's body on Wednesday.
On Sunday a four-year-old boy drowned while playing in a culvert along the Assiniboine River which drains into the Red.

"We've had some significant rises on the Red River in the last 24 hours, 1-1/2 to two feet from Emerson to Morris and three to 4-1/2 feet from Ste. Agathe to the (Winnipeg) Floodway due to high tributary inflows," Manitoba Natural Resources flood liaison engineer Larry Whitney told reporters.

About 17,000 residents of the Red River Valley between the U.S. border and Winnipeg were ordered out of their homes early on Wednesday, Manitoba Emergency Management Organization executive director Harold Clayton said.
Five hundred Winnipeggers with homes on low ground were ordered out of their homes on Tuesday, Winnipeg Streets and Transportation spokesman Bob McDonald said.

The city's floodway, a 29-mile long (47 km), 30-foot deep (9-metre) crescent-shaped drainage ditch around the eastern edge of Winnipeg should protect most of the city's more than 630,000 residents from flooding, Whitney said.
A dike around the Floodway was raised 4.5 feet (1.5 metres) to ensure the cresting Red River did not wash over the ditch.
"If the dike is breached, there will be flooding in the city, but I don't anticipate the probability of that happening to be very high," McDonald said. "I don't think that's very likely."
More than three million sandbags were laid across southern Manitoba and a 15-mile (24 km) long sandbag dike was extended southwest of Winnipeg to protect other homes, Clayton said.
Emergency officials, however, admitted they were not sure enough bags could be supplied to homeowners at risk.
"I was told last night I might have to evacuate. Better safe than sorry, I guess. If I can get extra sandbags I will. I don't know if I can get any," said Winnipeg resident Rob Diziak.

The Canadian government put 10 military helicopters and 17 zodiac boats at Manitoba's disposal. Some 355 soldiers were deployed filing sandbags and building dikes as 585 other troops were due to arrive, Clayton said.
Manitoba declared a state of emergency on Tuesday, giving provincial officials sweeping powers to seize property, put people to work on flood projects and force people from homes.
Flood crests were revised to reach the Canada-U.S. border on Monday, halfway to Winnipeg, at Morris on May 2 and Winnipeg on May 5, Whitney said.
Floods in 1950 and 1979 left 400 square miles (1,036 sq km) of land between the U.S. border and Winnipeg under water. This year's flood may cover double that area.
Railway companies shut Red River Valley lines on Wednesday as farmers trucked 17,000 hogs, 1,000 beef cattle, 200 dairy cows and 140,000 poultry out of the flood zone.
